utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber wishes to greet all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the staff of this courtroom, as well as those outside this courtroom. On this rainy morning, we will continue the hearing devoted to documents. Yesterday we were not able to fully complete the agenda, which consisted of three points, so we still have to address the question of relevance; however, yesterday the Defence indicated that they intended to refer to a number of documents. We have received only a few minutes ago a list drawn up by the Defence teams for both accused, and contrary to what was said yesterday, there are far fewer documents than we expected. Nevertheless, we do have a certain number of documents which are fully referenced in relation to the consolidated list of the Prosecution. It begins with number 38 -- 3538, and it ends with number 639. This is the document provided to us by the Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzihasanovic, and on behalf of Mr. Kubura, Mr. Dixon has also provided us with a list of documents. It was my understanding that the late arrival of this list could cause some problems for the Prosecution. That is why I should like to give the floor to Mr. Withopf, for him to explain to us the difficulties he may have and what his suggestion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. President, it's unfortunately a fact that both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution were only supplied -- were supplied with the list detailing the documents which Defence wishes to discuss today at a very late stage yesterday. Yesterday night at 6.54 p.m. I received an e-mail, the same e-mail which was addressed to the Chamber's legal officer, in which the Defence for the accused Hadzihasanovic listed 36 documents they in the course of the today's court session wish to discuss. At 6.30 p.m. yesterday night I have made inquiries with the Kubura Defence, which has-- which has promised on the record yesterday at about 2.00 that the list would be available -- would be made available within an hour. At 6.30, at my -- as a result of my inquiries, I was orally informed about the number of 18 documents they wish to discuss. The list of the Hadzihasanovic Defence counsel, Mr. President, Your Honours, followed the numbering system in the Prosecution's further detailed exhibit list; whereas, the basis for the today's discussion is the contested exhibit list. It took me more than one hour to actually figure out which documents Defence wishes to discuss, and it took me a bit more time to locate these documents in the binders. Once I had located them, Mr. President, Your Honours, I realised that there are a significant number of documents amongst them, amongst the documents Defence wishes to discuss - and that's again under the theme of poor photocopies and/or illegible signature. Defence counsel, both Defence counsel, made the information and made the list available to the Prosecution at a point in time it made it impossible for the Prosecution to properly prepare for the today's court session. Proper preparation would have required to discuss whatever issues may be discussed by Defence today with investigators and analysts. The main issue, however - and this refers to the issue of poor photocopies or illegible signature - is the fact that we can only discuss these documents once we have the originals in front of us, and the Prosecution, as Defence counsel are very well aware of, the Prosecution at 8.30 at night is not in a position to get the documents from the evidence vault. That means between 20.30 hours and 9.00 this morning the Prosecution was not in a position to see the documents and to properly prepare for the today's court session. In this context, Mr. President, I wish to refer to the declaration of Mr. Robert Reid, which has been handed over yesterday, paragraph 7, which describes that "During the scanning and optical character recognition process, portions of the image may be lost," obviously a potential that any printouts from the electronic system may be, in terms of quality, worse than the original, which may be a bad one anyway. Due to the fact that we received this information very late yesterday night, I'm not in a position to assist the Trial Chamber in its final determination on the issue of the selected documents to the extent I would have been in a position in the event I would have got the list earlier on, and I would have expected to be informed in due time. I wish to express my serious -- my serious concern about this matter, and I do request -- I do request the discussion on the selected documents to be -- to be postponed to tomorrow. I make reference to the situation on the ECMM documents. We had a very similar situation and Defence was granted sufficient time for preparation, and I think the same principles should apply for the Prosecution as well. This is a very unfortunate situation, since it's a waste of court time, and it is a solely and unnecessary cost by the Defence. I tried to find another -- a different solution yesterday night, but I cannot be professionally be prepared to the extent I wish to to discuss these documents for the reasons I outlined. At the very least, the Prosecution reserves its right to at a later point in the course of these proceedings to make additional observations. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. The Chamber has listened to your explanations. You have told us that you received the list late and that you were not able to identify the -- and find the original documents, to check the various points, and to prepare yourself for the adversarial debate that would necessarily ensue, and you are suggesting that we address this matter concerning the list of documents tomorrow. While you were speaking, I took my calculator and I listed 36 documents coming from the Hadzihasanovic Defence and 16 from Mr. Kubura's Defence. I note, unless I am mistaken, that there appear to be two documents that appear on both lists, documents 8 and 123, which means that the debate will have to address a total of 50 documents. So it's much less than we originally anticipated. The Judges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges, therefore, fully agree that the debate on the documents take place tomorrow, so we'll talk about the documents tomorrow, the 50 documents. It would be desirable, however, it seems to me, that the Prosecution tomorrow have in their possession the originals of the documents, which of course exist, and then in the course of the debate we can actually visualise the original documents. Why? You all know in view of your professional experience that a photocopied document does not fully reflect the original of the document. When we are talking about orders coming from the army, there are stamps; sometimes stamps are in colour; the colour does not appear, though of course there are photocopies in colour as well. But in view of the limited resources of the Prosecution, they cannot scan in colour. The colour can be indicative. A document has indicia of reliability if the stamps correspond fully. So there lies the interest in seeing the original document. Of course, it would have been preferable in a more general context that the originals be filed and not copies, but that is perhaps an idealistic approach. But when we are talking about documents, it is the original that should be tendered, for it is the original on the basis of which one should have a debate. So, Mr. Withopf, could you come tomorrow with the originals in your hand. That would be a good thing. Can the Prosecution tell us whether they will in fact be able to come with the originals tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if this request is limited to the 50 or so documents the Defence wishes to discuss tomorrow, I anticipate that this would be possible. If the request is, however, extended to all documents, that would be a bit of a challenge, since each and every single document has to be requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Let us satisfy ourselves with the 50 documents which we are going to have the debate about on the basis of the original copies. That would already be the first step. For if we have the original, we can better judge the quality of the typewriters used to type these orders and generally a better understanding of the documents. So one could call these external indicia of reliability. So tomorrow we will examine these documents. It would also be desirable, Mr. Withopf, the first six or seven documents come from binder number 1, so it would also be desirable for you to tell us in which binder which document can be found so that we can trace them more easily. This shouldn't be a big problem for the handling of these documents. Leaving aside this question of documents for the moment, we could still continue the discussion on the topics that still remain on the agenda; that is, the question of relevance, the more general problems linked to Rule 89(D). I see "general," though we'll see what the Defence will tell us about the documents. And they may say that if the documents are considered admissible, they may say that this is prejudicial to the accused pursuant to Rule 89(D), but that is just an assumption on my part. Nevertheless, we have to address 89(D) in general terms, which you did refer to in your filing, as several documents in column L, there's an indication of R89(D). So the Defence will give us their views in general terms of how they see 89(D). And the third topic would be linked to the question of the documents which need to be tendered through a witness in the opinion of the Defence. Perhaps they won't say 500 documents, because that would be pointless, but after having thought it over, the Defence perhaps could tell us that with respect to certain documents, those can be introduced only through a witness. By way of an example, let me mention the withdrawn witness, (redacted), whose documents were to be tendered during his testimony. And I think that is a possibility. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Thank you. We are now going to address the third topic, and that is the topic of relevance, unless Mr. Bourgon wishes to intervene on other issues before we address relevance. You have the floor, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Madam Judge. Good morning, Your Honour. Mr. President, the Prosecution has just made certain allegations regarding the behaviour of the Defence in preparation for this morning's hearing. It is difficult to respond to these allegations, which we see to be rather serious and absolutely unfounded. However, we feel it is our duty to do so. So, first of all, I shall address the question of numbering on the list provided to the Prosecution. Last week, Mr. President, the Defence made a suggestion to the Prosecution to exchange the electronic list of documents; that is, the lists that were submitted both by the Defence and the Prosecution, so that we can make a joint table of the two lists. The Prosecution accepted our suggestion. We exchanged electronic lists. We drew up a joint table that I have in front of me. And this table does not include the new numbering of contested exhibits. This is the first time -- the first time we saw this numbering was yesterday. When we received those documents, we noticed that a new system of numbering existed, because in front of each item there was a page saying "Prosecution number, contested exhibit." We used the numbers that were before the Chamber always, either the internal number of the Prosecution, the PT number, or the ERN numbers, and we continued to use that numbering until yesterday morning, when we received the list of the Prosecution, which was amended and which contained this new numbering of contested exhibits. Therefore, the use of this list does not provoke any confusion or delay and that it is very easy to refer to the documents identified by the Defence. We feel it is a minor point. What is more important, Mr. President, is that yesterday the list of documents were given to the Prosecution between 6.00 and 7.00 p.m. in writing by us and orally by the other Defence team. However, we have to see what the point of those lists were. They were never a condition, a precondition. The aim of the list was twofold: First, to allow the Defence to reduce the number of exhibits to be discussed to avoid any waste of time. And yesterday I told the Chamber that we had more than 80 documents but that we would do our best to reduce the number of exhibits so as to save time, and to be certain that we can complete the discussion on time, and that is what we did. When my learned friend telephoned at 6.30 p.m. yesterday, I told him, "I'm working on it. I'm almost done." From the end of the hearing, we worked hard to reduce the list and to act in a professional manner and with all due diligence. The second reason for this list was to allow everyone to be able to select the document from the binder and to be ready for this morning. There was never a question of preparing the list in advance. These hearings have been planned a long time ago, and the Prosecution should have been ready yesterday and today to discuss each of the documents that is in front of this Chamber. Today the Prosecution tells us that they are not ready to discuss the documents and they are endeavouring, which is rather disturbing for us, that this is the fault of the Defence. It is not the fault of the Defence. So, Mr. President, we should like to underline an important detail. My learned friend said that he needed time to bring all the documents to the Chamber. It is true that we discussed some 50 documents, but the Defence underlined that it is not a short list of contested documents but it is an example to allow the Chamber to make a determination on all the contested documents. So these are just examples which the Chamber could use when making its ruling. So the list of contested documents has not been reduced. Finally, Mr. President, we quite agree with the Chamber that we continue with the oral arguments on the two topics. I think that we can cover relevance and then address the two other points, 89(D) as well as the need for calling witnesses. And I think that these two topics can be addressed together and covered quickly so that both parties can be ready for tomorrow's hearing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just for the record, I do wish to clarify that the Defence team for Mr. Kubura sent an e-mail yesterday to your legal officer and to Mr. Withopf of the Prosecution at 17.14. I have a copy of the e-mail here in front of me, Your Honours. Unfortunately, the name of Mr. Withopf was spelt incorrectly and that's why the e-mail didn't reach him at 17.14. It did reach Your Honours' legal officer at that time, and it was as a result of that that a phone call was made by my learned friend to myself and I gave him the numbers over the phone to ensure that he had the documents and the information about them as soon as possible. I just wish to make that clear for the record, because we did try and ensure that the information was imparted as quickly as possible. And I do also wish to add that I am, like my learned friend Mr. Bourgon, somewhat surprised by the Prosecution raising this issue when it is really a matter of them having the responsibility of explaining to Your Honours, as Your Honours have said on many occasions, why all of these documents should be introduced. They have been asked to come to Court with all their documents, and the onus is on them to explain why these documents are authentic and why they are relevant. In relation, for example, to the illegible documents, we -- we indicated in our first response many weeks ago which were the illegible documents, and Your Honours ordered the Prosecution to explain why documents were illegible. This is just one example. But in the responses that were given yesterday, there were many questions left unanswered by the Prosecution, and that's one of the main reasons why we've chosen as illustrations some documents, Your Honour, to show Your Honours what we believe the problems to be, not only to leave it at the theoretical level but to refer to certain documents as examples in order to try and move the process forward. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Dixon, in the numbers that you have mentioned in your list, 4, 6, 8, 9, are these numbers the same as those of Mr. Bourgon and are they the same numbers as the ones the Prosecutor has in regard to the OTP -- with regard to the OTP number? Is it the same column as the one the Prosecutor has? I think that is the case, but could you confirm this for me, because number 4 -- take number 4 as an example. What does it correspond to, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct. We have used the contested exhibit number, which is the first number on the Prosecution's consolidated list. It's the number that appears on the front of each exhibit, so that it's absolutely clear which -- which document we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just a slight clarification, Mr. Dixon. You said that it was at 17.14. The document says "6.14." Is it a matter of GMT time in your document? Your document says "18.14" and not "17.14."

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the copy of the e-mail that I have, yes, is 17.14, and I do recall that it was at that time, at 15 minutes past 5.00 yesterday afternoon that we did send the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the document I have, it says "6.14," not "17.14." The legal officer will show you that it says "6.14." The usher will show you. You have "17.14" noted; I have "6.14" noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could exchange this document for the one I'm getting to indicate why I mention 17.14, which was the time that we did send the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, in fact the document that you have says "17.14," and my document says "6.14." There's a mystery. You're quite right. The document with "17.14" is the one I've shown you, but it also says "6.14." There's something mysterious here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Well, it's probably the clock in the computer which is set for one time and the other computer is set for a different time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a problem of summertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm that when the e-mail was sent, I was present, that it was sent at 17.14. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in your opinion, you think that the document can -- consider your document to be reliable . The Chamber can consider the document to be reliable. I think that the Prosecution wanted time for tomorrow, Mr. Bourgon, not because of the delay but I think it is a matter of substance -- matters of substance that they wanted to raise. Mr. Withopf, would you like to respond to this, or would you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confirm that the Trial Chamber has said? You want time to prepare yourself for the case -- for the sake of the substance, not because of the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may please very briefly respond to this issue. After the submission of my learned colleagues, the facts remain the same: The Prosecution got the list very late yesterday night. Unfortunately, due to the wrong spelling of my name, I haven't received any e-mail from the Kubura Defence yesterday. It was made very clear from the first beginning by the Trial Chamber that categories of documents would be discussed and not particular documents; therefore, there was no need for the Prosecution at any point in time to prepare for each and every single document, as Defence is suggesting. "Categories" was the key word. Therefore, I certainly disagree with any suggestion by my learned friends from the Defence that the Prosecution should have been in a position to discuss each and every single document to each and every extent necessary. I'm certainly in a position to, in compliance with the Trial Chamber's request, to discuss the categories and I'm certainly in a position and I'm very well prepared to discuss all three issues which are on the agenda today. I am, however, due to the fact that I got the list only very late yesterday night, I am not in a position to assist the Trial Chamber to the extent I would like to in respect to the particular documents which need to be discussed at the particular and at the specific request of Defence counsel. Therefore, I again request postponement of the discussion for these documents until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the documents are concerned, as has been said, we'll discuss them tomorrow. So we can address the issue of relevance, which is of crucial importance. I'll now give the floor to Mr. Withopf, who will present his explanations about relevance, which would allow him to tender all these documents into evidence. If he intends to tender these documents into evidence, it is because he believes all these documents to be relevant. So this is what we would like to hear Mr. Withopf comment on, and then the Defence will present its views on the relevance of the documents concerned. And naturally, if the issue of relevance has to be dealt with on the basis of individual documents, this will be done tomorrow. We can then deal with the documents in question. Mr. Withopf, you may proceed to comment on the issue of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm going to address the issue of relevance following the challenges Defence counsel have made in that respect. Defence quite often in some sort of stereotype statements has contested the relevance of documents for a number of reasons, including - and these appear to be the four main reasons - number one, outside the time frame of the indictment or the same reason but a different language only, irrelevant by virtue of date; number two, external to 3rd Corps and 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade; the third issue, the third challenge is not connected to allegations contained in the indictment, or phrased differently, sometimes irrelevant in substance; and number four, lacking information in respect to the sending and/or receiving of the document. Mr. President, Your Honours, the first two issues have already been addressed, at least partially yesterday in respect to the time frame of the indictment and any documents that are external to 3rd Corps and 7th Muslim Brigade. Therefore, I may please briefly summarise the Prosecution's position on these two issues. Outside the time frame of the indictment. This general observation, in the view of the Prosecution, must be rejected for a number of reasons. And I'm going to explain the reasons. Defence is limiting -- is limiting the period of the indictment to the period between the first crime-base incident, which was Dusina on the 26th of January, 1993, and the last crime-base incident, which was Vares in early November 1993. In the view of the Prosecution, this doesn't appear to be the right approach, in particular not in the context of a case which is based on responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Mr. President, Your Honours, I am going to give you a number of examples. The issue of any proposed exhibits or proposed documents before to the crime base, prior to the first crime-base incident in the indictment. Any issues in relation to notice and knowledge can be proven based on documents that show that the one or the other accused did know that there were problems with certain military units or certain elements within military units under their command. The accused Hadzihasanovic was the 3rd Corps commander from 14 November 1992 onwards. The accused Kubura was the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade Chief of Staff from 1st January 1993 onwards and the assistant chief of staff for operations and instruction matters from 11th December 1992 onwards. In exactly -- in exactly these capacities, both accused got to know about certain facts which will help the Prosecution to establish that they had notice and knowledge of facts, which in our view are related to aspects of failure to prevent and/or to punish. A second issue that relates to any documents which have a date that is prior to 26 of January, 1993. Such documents - and there are quite a few ones - which show the establishment of certain military units that do fall within the command structure of the accused, in particular the accused Hadzihasanovic, are relevant because they touch at the very least on the issue of superior and subordinate relationship. If I may, please, show one example. The issue of the subordination of the Mujahedin. It's the Prosecution's case that the Mujahedin arrived starting from August 1992 onwards, and it's the Prosecution's case that the Mujahedin were incorporated within the 3rd Corps structures after its establishment on 18 August 1992, after the takeover of command of 3rd Corps by the accused Hadzihasanovic on 14 November 1992, and after the subordination of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade on 19 November 1992. These are all dates outside the indictment period as defined by Defence and such documents are obviously of high relevance. I already yesterday, Mr. President, Your Honours, addressed the issue of the responsibility to punish. The responsibility and the duty to punish doesn't end with the last crime-base incident. This responsibility and duty continues at the very least as long as the accused were in a position to punish, meaning having had a command function resulting in a superior-subordinate relationship. This applies to both accused, in particular, however, to the accused Kubura, who was commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade until mid-March 1994. It is the Prosecution's submission that the time frame of the indictment as defined and limited by the Defence can be an indicator as to whether documents are relevant or irrelevant. It depends on the concrete contents of such documents. In order to finish my submission in respect to this particular aspect in respect to relevance, I wish to show an example which shows the absurdity of the Defence position. If today somebody from within 3rd Corps would write me a letter dated the 28th of April, 2004 and in this letter would admit a number of crimes that do fall within the indictment period, 1993, and informing me about the fact that he had informed the one or the other accused about these crimes in all detail, if one would follow the Defence submission and the Defence suggestion, such a letter, such a document would not be relevant under the criteria "irrelevant by virtue of date. " If I may move on, Your Honours, to the second Defence concern or challenge; namely, external to 3rd Corps HQ and 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. This issue has also already touched upon yesterday. I am making reference to what we said in the course of the yesterday's court session. To further elaborate on this issue, however - and I will again show examples that show the full -- or show how problematic such an approach appears to be - there is number 181 of the list, which is number 90 on the list with the contested documents; there is an interview with the accused Hadzihasanovic, which Defence identified as external to 3rd Corps HQ and 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. For the sake of the correctness of the transcript, I, however, wish to mention that the box "relevance" is not ticked by the Defence. This argument, however, has been used for a number of documents which Defence considers not being relevant. In the course of the interview I just mentioned, the accused Hadzihasanovic was asked by the interviewer on 1st of December, 1993: Question: You are one of the most experienced officers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the command and control of units in such fighting." And the accused answers by saying: "That's right." Obviously relevant, Mr. President, Your Honours. And in the same interview the accused Hadzihasanovic gives a full account of his military career; again obviously relevant. I see my learned colleague on his feet. He may have any observation to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to note, as my colleague has said, the box concerning relevance wasn't ticked in the case of this document, so I really don't see what the relevance of my colleague's arguments is. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do continue, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And as I said, I have made for the sake of the correctness of the transcript this observation for myself. If I may, please, address the third issue, the third challenge by the Defence, not connected to allegations contained in the indictment or phrased differently sometimes, irrelevant in substance. The Prosecution in its filing of 19 April 2004 has detailed the relevance of such documents in making reference to specified paragraphs in the indictment. I am explicitly making reference to this filing. What I, however, wish to emphasise -- what we wish to emphasise again is that this case is obviously a circumstantial case in many areas -- in many areas related to evidentiary issues. This includes in particular all matters related to Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. This implies that a document, that based on a view focussing on one single document only, such an approach may lead to the conclusion that this particular document may not be relevant. However, this case is a case which puts together bits and pieces and pieces of a puzzle to a broader picture and the broader picture in the view of the accused -- in the view, sorry, of the Prosecution will show the guilt of the accused. Therefore, any document - and we wish to emphasise this again - can only be judged upon after having reviewed all other documents and series of documents, as I mentioned yesterday, may be a very particular issue in this case. The fourth main challenge, or the fourth main concern by Defence was lacking information in respect to the sending and/or receiving of the document. This criteria, in the submission of the Prosecution, Mr. President, Your Honours, can -- can't be one to be used in the determination of the relevance of a document. The fact that a document is lacking such information can touch upon the probative value only; the relevance, however, is not concerned. Again, just an example to illustrate this: If there is an order of one of the accused requesting information in respect to a certain allegation that a crime may have been committed, such a document is obviously relevant in order to prove that the respective accused had notice and knowledge of the crime, at the very least inquiry knowledge. In the submission of the Defence, such a document should not be admitted into evidence if it does not contain a statement as to whether it had been sent and/or received. In the view of the Prosecution, this can't be true for the only reason that if a document is signed by the accused, it proves irrespective as to whether the document was sent or received, irrespective of this fact that the respective accused had knowledge of such crimes. Again, thinking through all four challenges, through all four aspects of the challenges of Defence, it appears that they are not really convincing ones. I would be prepared, Mr. President, Your Honours, to continue with any issues related to Rule 89(D); however, I understand the Trial Chamber wants first to give the Defence an opportunity to respond on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will give the floor to the Defence. But as I usually do, I would like to summarise the position you have expressed to make everything clear for everyone; in particular, for those who are following these proceedings on the outside. As far as the relevance is concerned, the Prosecution mentioned four items: Firstly, they mentioned the time frame referred to in the indictment; secondly, they mentioned documents that are external to the 3rd Corps; the third point concerned the fact that no reference is made to the allegations contained in the indictment; and the fourth point concerns the lack of information. With regard to the time frame in the indictment, Mr. Withopf pointed out that the 26th of January in Dusina is when the time frame starts and continues up until November 1993 in Vares, but the charges and Article 7(3) of the Statute provide, as far as the penal responsibility of a superior is concerned, provides that a superior has to punish and prevent crimes and such prevention must take place before the violation is committed. So an offence committed on the 26th of January -- in the case of an offence committed on the 26th of January means that the Prosecution will naturally have to base itself on what happened before -- will have to refer to what happened before that date. And in addition, protective measures have to be taken - and this is the responsibility of the superior - such measures must necessarily take place after the event itself, after the crime itself. So the Prosecution provided us with an example: Imagine the Prosecution receiving a letter from someone who mentions crimes committed, for example, in Dusina or elsewhere. According to the Defence's theory, this letter would have no relevance. The Prosecution provided this example to show that the arguments concerning the time frame referred to in the indictment can't be accepted. With regard to the second point, documents that are external to the 3rd Corps, the Prosecution told us that the Defence's approach is very problematic and the Prosecution gave as an example the interview given by one of the accused. This interview, even if it didn't come from the 3rd Corps -- but if the interview was given by someone from the 3rd Corps, you could consider him to be integrated within the 3rd Corps; but even if it was from the 3rd Corps, the Prosecution tells us that you could consider the interview to be relevant on the basis of its substance, and as far as documents external to the 3rd Corps are concerned, it's necessary to take into consideration, take into account the content. That's the second point. As far as the third point is concerned, it's true that the Defence with regard to the lack of references to the indictment, we were told that the allegations weren't contained in the indictment, is what the Defence stated. The Prosecution has claimed that in the documents that it has listed, each document in the column concerning relevance contains references to the relevant paragraph in the indictment. As an example, document number 1, which was contested, reference for that document is paragraph 17 - 20. So the Prosecution has told us that in its document they made reference to all appropriate references in the indictment. And the next point concerns the lack of information. The Defence orally informed us, but also in writing, that the documents didn't have the dates when the document was sent, received, didn't mention the addressees, et cetera, so there was certain information missing. Mr. Withopf has said - and the Defence will respond to what he has said - that the question of sending and receiving a document is a secondary question in relation to the contents of the document itself. The Prosecution provided us with an example: Let's imagine that there is an order issued by one of the accused requesting that certain investigations be launched or requesting information if a crime was committed. In such a case, the contents of the order itself prove that the accused was aware of a crime, and given the existence of this document, it's a relevant document. As far as the distribution of this document is concerned or the reception of this document, in view of the Prosecution, this is a minor problem in relation to the contents of the document, since the contents of the document show that the person who drafted the order was aware of an event or requested information about the event concerned. So in general terms, this is the Prosecution's position in relation to the four points that relate to relevance. The Defence will express its position, since the Prosecution has presented us with detailed explanations concerning the time frame in the indictment and their position was very specific and they provided examples with regard to the other points. Who will be the first person to intervene? I think it will be Mr. Bourgon, who has just taken his headphones off. And as this will take some time, as his presentation will be lengthy, he is preparing himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The arguments of the Defence regarding relevance, Mr. President, will not be very lengthy. For us relevance is one of the factors that appears in Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which says that: "A document is admissible if it is both relevant and has a minimum of probative value." Yesterday in the course of my submissions, I gave you a definition of "relevance", as can be found in the Delalic ruling, which says that: "Relevance is the relationship that exists between two facts and when the probative value would be the tendency of evidence to establish the case for which it is called by the Prosecution." Once again, we refer to the Delalic decision, which tells us that at the stage of admissibility, the standard shouldn't be too high, because it is up to the Judges to attach the weight they wish to a document subsequently. In the opinion of the Defence, Mr. President, there are three criteria that can assist the Chamber to establish whether a minimum level of relevance has been attained at the admissibility stage. First of all, there's the question of substance. Does the document proposed have any connection with the proposition that the Prosecution is trying to establish? Then we also come to the question of time; that is, whether a document proposed deals with an element occurred [as interpreted] prior to the indictment or after the ratione temporis of the indictment. Finally, the third criteria in connection with relevance is when the reliability of the document is so weak that it affects relevance; this is drawn again from the Delalic decision of 1996. As you have been able to note, Mr. President, in our list we make very few challenges regarding the relevance of documents and we have adopted a highly liberal approach to this subject, especially with respect to substance. Virtually all the documents contested by the Defence on grounds of relevance were contested on the grounds of the time. If we're talking about the army and roughly the time period, then it's fine. So our approach was very -- a very liberal one, and we contested very few documents on the grounds of a link between the fact established and the point that the Prosecution wishes to make. Regarding the time frame, we have challenged a number of documents, and I mention as an example a quick list of documents which the Defence is contesting on the grounds of relevance because of the time. There's document 51 or PT53. I'm using the internal numbering of the Prosecution as well as the PT numbers. That is the list I've been working with from the beginning. Exhibit 116 or PT120, Exhibit 117, 118, 119, 123, 180, 187, 201, 210, 214, 251, 292, 310, 339, 386, 387, and 808, 809, 810, 811, 826, 849, and finally 934 to 944. Those are the documents which the Defence is contesting on the grounds of relevance because of the date of the document, of the time frame. Regarding the other points addressed by my learned friend, I would specifically address the question of time frame and date because that is the main issue raised by my colleague from the Prosecution. The Defence would refer to a ruling concerning 7(3) of the Statute, and that is that there is a link between the date when a person occupied a command position and his responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. So a person may have been aware of a fact on a date prior to the indictment, but that person at that point in time did not hold a command position. And what is even more important is the period after the indictment. By way of example: The accused General Hadzihasanovic was no longer commander of the 3rd Corps and no longer had a command position as of the 1st of November, 1993. From that date onwards, his responsibility regarding all offences committed within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina changes. To use the example given by my learned friend: If today in 2004 General Hadzihasanovic was still a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and were to receive today a letter containing an admission regarding a crime committed in 1993, certainly in the sense of law, strictly speaking he has a certain responsibility with respect to that letter, but his responsibility in the context of the position that he held in 1993 are no longer a command position. So if a person receives such a letter in 2004 and does nothing with that letter, he could easily be charged but of another offence that would not stem from Article 7(3) of the Statute. That is the temporal plane strictly speaking. But there's also a question of substance. If General Hadzihasanovic on the 1st of November, 1993 was no longer the commander and no longer had the means, the ability to take reasonable and necessary steps to prevent or to punish, then that is an important distinction, but especially if the Chamber focuses on the documents proposed by the Prosecution, one must see the events that those documents address, to what extent that is linked to the ability to prevent or punish. And for these reasons, Mr. President, the number of documents Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that I referred to a moment ago are mostly -- refer to dates that occurred after General Hadzihasanovic changed his position, and that was on the 1st of November, 1993. Regarding the second point raised by my colleague, that is, documents external to the 3rd Corps, we submit, Mr. President, that this is not related to the relevance of documents and the argument proffered by my colleague. In our opinion, the fact that the date of a document -- that a document is external to the 3rd Corps has nothing to do with relevance, but it is a very important point. A third point was the links to the allegations. Is there a link between the indictment and those events? As I have said, the Defence adopted a highly liberal approach and for us, if a document deals with the army in general and the 3rd Corps during the time frame of the indictment, for us it has a sufficient degree of relevance for the document to be admitted. But as we have said, there may be other problems with that document. Finally, the fourth and last point, Mr. President, regarding the lack of information. Once again, Mr. President, we quite agree that the lack of information on a document has nothing to do with relevance and that was not our submission. We did say yesterday, however - and we wish to underline again - that the absence of information is a determining factor when deciding on the admissibility of a document. Finally, I should like to underline the practice of this Chamber with respect to relevance up to the present, because even though during our filings on criteria our approach was very liberal, we would like to point out that if we look at the exhibits admitted up to now - and by way of example, I refer to Exhibit DH44, DH45, DH47, DH48, 49, and 50 - these are exhibits, Mr. President, which are in the file marked for identification only. Why? Because the Prosecution challenged their relevance. We have to be coherent when we are talking about relevance and consistent. We wish to adopt a liberal approach. That's fine. But we feel that the Chamber should, when assessing the relevance of documents, bear in mind the arguments of the Prosecution with respect to relevance. In this connection, Mr. President, I should also like to refer to a Prosecution document dated the 23rd of March, 2004, in which the Prosecution submits its observations regarding questions of judicial notice of admitted facts in other cases. In that document, Mr. President, the Prosecution is proposing by way of example that the treatment of the civilian population by the enemy, the detention of military-age men, why such facts are of relevance. This is paragraph 32. Later on in paragraph -- they tell us: "Even if the HVO mistreated the civilian population, even if the HVO detained Muslim men of military age, how can those factors affect the responsibility of the accused and at best those facts are of no assistance to the Chamber." Later on we are told: "The preparation and the resources, the arming of their own forces and of the enemy forces are equally facts which are not relevant." I will stop there, Mr. President, simply to indicate that in spite of the liberal approach of the Defence regarding relevance, the Prosecution appears to have a far more restrictive approach to the same issue. And I think the Chamber should bear this in mind when rendering its ruling. A final comment, Mr. President, has to do with the relevance of facts. My colleague listed a number of examples during his submissions, but he said something of -- which is very interesting. He said, "We are in a circumstantial case," that evidence is circumstantial, which means that the Prosecution believes that they have no direct evidence that the accused did not fulfil their duty and did not take the reasonable and necessary steps to prevent or punish. This is something of the greatest importance, Mr. President, when determining the question of relevance of the facts submitted. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution will have occasion to respond to these points, but before I give the floor to Mr. Dixon, I shall nevertheless summarise your position so that we are quite clear about it. Regarding relevance, the jurisprudence that you rely on is 89(C) and the Delalic decisions when "relevance" is defined as follows: "Relevance is the relationship between two facts." And on that basis, you said that for you, when it comes to relevance, the standard should not be too high, but for a minimum standard at least three criteria have to be met, and that is whether the document proposed meets the criteria of time and reliability, and if a document is not reliable, it affects relevance. Regarding the minimum standard and the three criteria, you feel that you have adopted a highly liberal approach when it comes to relevance. And as an illustration of what you're saying, you indicate that in fact you did not challenge more than 35 documents. And I added up the numbers that you quoted, and that in your view the debate should focus, rather, on the question of the time frame, the period before and the period after. And by way of example, as an argument of substance, you say that your client was no longer at the head of the 3rd Corps as of the 1st of November, 1993. So you're illustrating your submissions with this very precise fact, and that is that he was no longer the commander of the 3rd Corps after the 1st of November, 1993. As for the three other points addressed by the Prosecution - that is, documents external to the 3rd Corps - you do not challenge them. In fact, one could say that globally you are in agreement. As for the third point that has to do with allegations related to the indictment, here again your stand is quite open-minded and liberal. And as for the fourth point on the shortages in the documents, you say that it is up to the Chamber to judge but that for you this question is not directly linked to relevance, that is, the missing information on documents. And finally, with regard to relevance, you have taken a liberal approach, and to contradict the Prosecution you tell us that they did not adopt a similar approach because they objected to your tendering documents DH44, 45, 47, 48, 49 and 50 because those documents which were marked for identification were not relevant in the opinion of the Prosecution. You also underlined the fact that the Prosecution could be contradicting itself in view of the written filings by it in the motion with respect to judicial notice of certain facts, in which the Prosecution - and you mentioned examples - appears to be in contradiction with what it is submitting. But generally, to summarise your position, you are telling us that you adopted a liberal approach but that in fact for you the main debate is on ratione temporis, that the time frame is important for you, and that you tell us that as of the 1st of November, 1993 your client cannot be charged with anything because he no longer held a command position. This would be a summary of your submissions mainly for the people watching these proceedings. I will now give the floor to Mr. Dixon, who will certainly also address the question of time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm conscious of the time, Your Honour. I will be a little bit longer than two or three minutes, and it might be better to have a break first. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber was so engrossed in expectation of what you were going to tell us that I forgot the time. You brought us back to reality, and that is why I shall have to interrupt the hearing for technical reasons, and we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume. And Mr. Dixon can take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On the topic of relevancy, Your Honours, the first point which we wish to make is that we are somewhat at a loss as to why, even though the Prosecution has been given an opportunity to explain the relevance of the documents, and that was indeed Your Honours' order, that they should explain why the documents are relevant, today we still have not heard from the Prosecution why documents and why particular documents are relevant to the case. Your Honours will recall that we noted when this matter first arose that only just over 200 documents were listed in the Prosecution pre-trial brief which are now on the contested list of exhibits, where some explanation was given for why the document was relevant. In many cases, in our view, an insufficient explanation, sometimes simply a footnote, but nevertheless the document was referred to within the context of the allegations the Prosecution has to prove. So we are still waiting for their explanations for the other 400 or so documents, as to why they are relevant. The Prosecution did in its submission -- written submission refer to certain paragraphs of the indictment for different documents. However, Your Honours will in all likelihood note that those are very general paragraphs that are referred to. Sometimes all of the paragraphs within which the charges are located in the indictment are referred to. And in our submission, they do not assist us any further in understanding what is the Prosecution's case in respect of these documents. It may well be that some of them are referred to in the half-time submission response of the Prosecution or in the closing argument, but by that stage the Prosecution would have closed its case and also the Defence, certainly in the case of the closing argument, would have presented its case as well. In our view, the burden lies on the Prosecution to set out what its case is in relation to these documents and that we would then be in a position to respond in more detail. Your Honour, the applicable Rule - it's been mentioned a few times for the admissibility of documents, and I do wish to refer to it again, given the question mark that was raised by Your Honours yesterday over my submission that probative value is essential as an ingredient at this stage of admissibility - is Rule 89(C), which says that: "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." So the Rule is, in our submission, very clear, Your Honour. In order to admit evidence, it has to be relevant, and it must be deemed to have probative value. Thereafter, the weight to be attached to the document or the extent of the value to be given to the document is a separate matter altogether. And as my learned friend has indicated, that may well depend on other documents and cross-referencing to other evidence. But when the document is looked at on its own, the test to be applied is whether it is relevant and whether it has probative value. Your Honours -- and in our submission of the 19th of April, when we filed a response to the Prosecution consolidated exhibit list, we set out there what we believe the test to mean; namely, that there must be a link established between the proposed exhibit and an issue which the Prosecution must prove as part of their case, an allegation or an element of the offence. There must be a link between the document and an issue that must be proved. And an issue that is indeed in dispute, there's no need to introduce documents about issues that are not disputed or that do not have to be adjudicated upon. And that secondly, the document has a value in that it can assist the Chamber in deciding upon that issue in dispute. In our submission, the threshold is not a very strict or higher one for the purposes of admissibility, but there is nevertheless a threshold, that of relevance and that of probative value. And in our view, the reason for that threshold is because we are in a unique system here, not a civil-law system, not a common-law system, if we were in a civil-law system, well, many of these problems would not arise, because as Your Honours are well aware, the investigating judge would have collected all these documents, and they would have officially and formally been brought into the case file, and the Prosecution and Defence would have been part of that process from the beginning. But we're not in that situation here. One of the parties in an adversarial system has collected these documents. The Defence and Your Honours were not part of that process, and hence there is a need to closely scrutinise the documents that we have before us and determine whether they meet the threshold of Rule 89(C). We're also not in a pure common-law system where it would be the usual practice to have a witness statement with each and every document or group of documents that is collected by the police and the Prosecution, with the Defence able to indicate whether they contest that material and whether it should be brought live before the jury or a trial judge. So in our submission, Your Honours, the need to closely observe the provisions of Rule 89(C) is paramount in a system which is not either one or other of the mainstream traditional procedural systems. Your Honour, to move on, then, to the specific categories of relevance. My learned friend, Mr. Bourgon, has once again touched on many of them in great detail. I don't wish to repeat what he has said. The one, of course, that is very important for Mr. Kubura is documents that are dated outside the time period of when he was in command or allegedly responsible for subordinates who may have committed offences. And that quite clearly is from 1 April 1993, not January but 1 April 1993, until - and the Defence doesn't dispute this - a point in time in early 1994. That is the time period within which he can be charged for offences allegedly committed by his subordinates. In our view, the Prosecution has misunderstood the submission we've made in this regard. We have never said that documents outside of that time period are as a matter of principle absolutely to be excluded. Our submission is that if a document is dated outside of the period of command, which is 1 April 1993 into early 1994, that is dated outside of that period, then it's for the Prosecution to show why that document is relevant to the period of command. In our view, that threshold must be relevant to the crimes that the Prosecution alleges were committed during the period of command when Mr. Kubura is able to be held responsible under the jurisprudence of the Trial Chamber. And I refer to the Appeals Chamber decision in this case on that point. So there has to be a clear nexus between documents outside of the time period of his command and crimes that were committed during the period of his command with which he is charged in the indictment. So Mr. Withopf is absolutely correct that if there was a confession in 1995 about crimes committed during the period of command, that document would be relevant and would be admissible. The Defence would have no objection to such a document being admitted. But the Prosecution doesn't have those kinds of documents. What the Prosecution has, for example, - and these are some of the documents we will refer to tomorrow - is a number of orders in January 1993 issued by Mr. Koricic, who was then the commander of the 7th Brigade, in relation to, for example, the music school. None of the alleged crimes in the music school are referred to in those orders. Mr. Kubura is not referred to in those orders. He's not even on the list of people to be sent those orders. And we are at a loss as to why it's necessary to introduce those documents when they are outside of the time period of Mr. Kubura's alleged command time and when they do not have any relevance to any of the alleged crimes, which, for example, the Prosecution say took place at the music school. And there are many such documents. There are documents that date even after 1994, in 1995, which on their face bear no connection to the alleged crime base. And in our view it is only fair and reasonable that those documents are excluded, unless the Prosecution can explain to us why it wishes to reply upon those documents, in which case the Defence will then be on notice as to what the relevance of the document is and we can prepare our defence accordingly. We requested that the Prosecution indicate what the relevance of those documents are. Your Honour, there are about 58, 59 of those documents which fall either before the period commencing 1 April 1993 or after early 1994, and we can provide a list of those so that it would make it a lot easier for Your Honours to be able to address those documents. I will tomorrow refer to -- to some of them by way of example to show the lack of relevance, in our submission. As the Prosecution has not indicated their relevance at this stage, we are of the view that those documents should be excluded. And that is our request, that at least those documents, the 59 or so documents, should be excluded. Your Honour, only one final matter for me to address, as the others have been sufficiently covered already, and that is the question of a circumstantial case which the Prosecution has indicated both yesterday and today. The danger, in our submission, of such an indication on the part of the Prosecution is that it can serve as a catch-all for any document. The list of documents that could be submitted, then, is potentially endless. It's a lot easier to say to Your Honours, "Well, this is a circumstantial case. There are many pieces in the puzzle. It will all fit together at some stage, and therefore everything should be introduced," just in case there is one little piece of evidence that might become relevant that is left out. And we can leave it all to the end to determine, and Your Honours might even exclude documents at the end. It's a lot easier to do that than to, at this stage, put down quite clearly what the Prosecution's case is, what are the pieces of the puzzle, and how do they fit together. If they are documents which the Prosecution wishes to hold in reserve, it's entirely possible, as has happened, for those documents to be left on the court file marked for identification. And if they do become relevant - either through the half-time submission - this is after the Prosecution has completed it case, or the Defence case, or the Prosecution has a chance to respond to the Defence case - and there's still an opportunity, of course, for Your Honours to call evidence as well - those documents could, then, become exhibits. But in our view, it's not sufficient to say, "Well, this is a case that involves a number of circumstances and inferences and therefore everything should just come in." A limit has to be put on it and we have to keep it in proportion, otherwise we are potentially in a situation where for any document the submission can be made, "Well, it might be relevant at some point, Your Honour, it's a circumstantial case." In our view, the Prosecution should pin their colours to the mast, say which are the documents that are most essential for their case, argue quite clearly why they are relevant. That will assist immeasurably in narrowing the issues - for Your Honours as well, when you have to adjudicate on the disputed matters - and the bulk of the documents, the remaining documents, can be left on the file to be referred to if and when necessary. Thank you, Your Honours. Those are our submissions on the point of relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I'll summarise what you have just said, as I did a while ago, and then the Prosecution will respond. First of all, you mentioned that the Prosecution did not explain why the documents that they want to tender were relevant. That was your starting point. You said that it was incumbent on the Prosecution to prove their case; they bear the burden of proof. We're in a hybrid system as far as proof is concerned. The procedure that we follow is not strictly speaking a common-law system or a civil-law system. It's a hybrid system, and in all such hybrid systems it's necessary to examine the Rules. The relevant Rule is 89(C). This is the Rule you referred to. This is the Rule that has to be taken into account when considering the relevance, admissibility, and probative value of documents. And, in fact, 89(C) says: "That a Chamber may admit any evidence which it deems to have probative value." You went on to say that it was necessary to respect - and these are your own terms - this Rule in a very strict fashion, and you requested that the Trial Chamber should assess the probative value of the documents concerned. As your colleague, Mr. Bourgon, you dealt with the issue of the time frame, the issue of orders, and with regard to your client, Mr. Kubura, you stressed the fact that orders issued in January could in no way concern your client. And you mentioned the music school by way of example. You pointed out that when we have a look at the list of documents, there are documents that are prior to and subsequent to the indictment, and you mentioned 58 or 59 of them. In your opinion, these documents should be excluded. It seems that you are contesting the Prosecution's thesis according to which the proof is constituted of elements of a puzzle that has to be put together, and it's only once the puzzle has been put together that it will be possible for the Trial Chamber to assess the probative value and relevance of the documents concerned. So in general terms, this is the position that you expressed, and you would like about 60 documents to be excluded, since they don't fall within the time frame referred to in the indictment. And you likewise stressed the fact that probative value was also at stake here. On the basis of what Mr. Bourgon and you yourself have said, the Prosecution will now take the floor to address the arguments presented by the Defence. Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will limit the reply to four distinct issues which arose during Defence counsel responding to our submission. Number one, I will discuss the issue of time frame; number two, I will discuss the practice of this Trial Chamber; number three, I will again very briefly address the issue of circumstantial evidence; and number four, I will certainly make a few remarks in respect to what has been said by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence in respect to how this can be dealt with once the trial reached the stage of the rebuttal. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Let me first address the issue of time frame. There is a situation prior to the indictment period, as defined by our learned friends from the Defence, and a situation after the indictment period. I may explain this again in respect to the accused Kubura; the same, however, would apply for the accused Hadzihasanovic as well. It's correct that the accused Kubura became acting commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade on 1st of April, 1992 and he became the commander at a later point in time. However, he earlier on already in 1992, in December 1992, held certain positions within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. He first was assistant chief of staff, and he then became the Chief of Staff on 1st January 1993. Defence for the accused Kubura is making reference to the Appeals Chamber decision. The Appeals Chamber decision addressed the issue as to whether the accused Kubura can be charged with crimes committed by his subordinates prior to 1st of April, 1993. This addresses the issue of charges. In our view, my learned friend from the Kubura Defence is missing the point. The Appeals Chamber decision has nothing to do with the issue of the admissibility of documents into evidence. Documents the Prosecution wishes to be tendered into evidence serve the purpose to prove facts that are related to the charges. Even if the Prosecution is based on the Appeals Chamber decision only allowed to charge the accused Kubura for crimes that were committed only at the time when a superior-subordinate relationship existed, any facts he got to know earlier on in his various positions within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, any such facts and any notice and knowledge can be relevant to his duty to prevent and to punish at a later stage of the proceedings or at a later stage once he received command. These are two separate issues, and they should be dealt with separately. If I may elaborate on the issue. It's the Prosecution's view that the whole issue can't be dealt with in abstracto. And I agree with my learned friends from the Defence, the documents have to be looked at document by document. However - and I come back to my example earlier on today - if such a letter from 28th of April, 2004 - and this touches on an issue that has been addressed by the Hadzihasanovic Defence - it doesn't matter that the accused Hadzihasanovic became the ABiH Chief of Staff on the 1st of November or maybe a few days later. That's not the point. In a letter dated 28th of April, 2004 evidence could be contained which shows that the accused Hadzihasanovic got to know about certain crimes - and I'm taking the example of Dusina - on the 27th of January, 1993. Again, the date -- the date in abstracto of a document, that can't be the criteria to be used to determine on the admissibility of documents. If I may, please, move on to the issue of the practice of the Trial Chamber which has been addressed by my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence. The practice of this Trial Chamber is liberal, and documents went into evidence dated outside the indictment period. The Defence has taken a broad interpretation of the Chamber's liberal approach in respect to all context-related issues. The Prosecution's point is, Mr. President, Your Honours, there's a difference between context and the charges in the indictment. The Prosecution wishes to tender into evidence documents which are relevant to the charges in the indictment. That has nothing or does not have not necessarily to do with the context [sic]. The Prosecution can't see any contradiction in its approach in respect to the admissibility of documents and its approach in respect to the issue of judicial notice. The third issue I wish to address, circumstantial evidence. I said and I stay -- stand by to it that this case is a case which in some areas - and in particular in respect to areas related to issues of Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute - is a circumstantial case, meaning that the evidence is circumstantial, meaning that bits and pieces of evidence must be put together in order to give the Prosecution an opportunity to assist the Trial Chamber in finding out the truth and to show the full picture. Therefore, it is of great importance that the materials are not looked at document by document but in their totality. The last issue I wish to address is the suggestion made by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence; namely, that the documents could be marked for identification, they could be on the court records, and the Prosecution would be given an opportunity to, in the rebuttal proceedings, try to tender these documents into evidence. The rebuttal proceedings, Mr. President, Your Honours, the rebuttal proceedings are governed by certain rules, and the rebuttal -- and such rules in respect to the rebuttal very strictly limit what the Prosecution can do in rebuttal. It only can address issues that came out during the presentation of the Defence case. The suggestion of my learned friend from the Kubura Defence would never enable the Prosecution in compliance with the Rules to tender such documents into evidence. Therefore, the Prosecution very strongly objects to any such suggestion. In this context - and I would have mentioned it later on in the today's proceedings, but it actually fits in the issue -- or within the issue of rebuttal - the Prosecution's suggestion would be a different one, and it's based on the -- it's based on the procedure which has been applied in the case against Kvocka. And I am referring to the decision of the 17th of March, 1999. That's the order granting request for admission of documentary evidence. What the Kvocka Trial Chamber applied is the following: The documents shall be admitted and it's up to the Defence whilst presenting their case to challenge the authenticity of any of the documents or to raise whatever issues, and then the Prosecution shall deal with any issues raised as to the authenticity in the course of its presentation in rebuttal. That would be the suggestion of the Prosecution, which is quite different from the suggestion by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence. For the time being, I do not want to go in any further detail. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, in general terms, you responded to the remarks of the Defence by referring to four points: The time frame, the practice of the Trial Chamber, the question of circumstantial evidence, and the remarks made by the Defence suggesting some new possibilities. Regarding the time frame, you stood by your position, recalling in a detailed way the functions held by General Kubura in 1992 and before the 1st of January, 1993. Therefore, with regard to the time frame, you tell us that what counts is not the date but in fact the contents of the document. As for the practice of the Chamber, you say this Chamber and other Chambers have always had an open approach and this needs no additional comment. As for circumstantial evidence, you also stand by what you said, and that is that there is -- there are bits and pieces of evidence which allow one to form a picture and that those fragments should be viewed in their totality. And by way of a suggestion, you say that these matters could be addressed during the rebuttal, as the Defence says, but you are absolutely opposed to that approach, that this cannot be addressed in rebuttal. You referred to the decision of the 17th of March, 1999 in the Kvocka case, and you are inviting the Chamber to take into consideration that decision. To sum up, you have not taken into account the arguments made by the Defence with respect to the question of time, and you stand by your original position. We have listened to you. Everyone had a chance to express their views. We had an adversarial debate on relevancy. And the Chamber will make its determination. We have the two other points remaining; that is, 89 -- but let me say in view of the position of the Prosecution, does the Defence have a replica to make? If you consider that to be of use, yes. But perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sure that that would be your position. Mr. Dixon, do you wish to respond to what Mr. Withopf said?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Just one clarification. I believe in the transcript the date of when Mr. Kubura was charged from wasn't indicated correctly. It's before 1 April 1993. That's when the bulk of the 60 documents that I referred to are dated. So it's 1 April 1993. And one final point, Your Honour, in respect of the rebuttal argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the rebuttal argument made by my learned friend. My submission was that there are many stages following the Prosecution case when documents could be admitted, including obviously the Defence stage, when through cross-examination of Defence witnesses documents could be put to those witnesses and authenticated and their relevance shown in that way. Likewise, when Your Honours -- if Your Honours so do, call witnesses, those witnesses can be examined by both of the parties. And in the -- the rebuttal stage itself, if there are issues that have arisen which make documents relevant because of the Defence case, then the Prosecution would be able to introduce those documents at that stage. And that would allow Your Honours to assess the documents document by document with a witness present and ensure that the proper threshold, as set out in Rule 89(C), was followed. And that was the essence of my submission, that this is not the end of it for these documents; they could be admitted at various stages once their relevance becomes known in the broader scheme of the evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dixon is explaining the question of rebuttal, saying that the procedure allows the Prosecution during the so-called rebuttal stage to present new documents linked to the debate at that point in time and that it is always possible at that stage for the Chamber to rule regarding the relevance of documents. That is a point that you have made. As I have indicated, we took note of everything that both parties have told us and we will make our determinations. The other two points we have on the agenda are 89(D), Rule 89(D), and also the questions linked to documents which can only be produced through a witness. These two points on the agenda, Mr. Bourgon wishes to combine them in a single presentation. Perhaps it would be better for the Defence to start with its observations, and then the Prosecution can respond, for us to proceed more effectively. Is Mr. Withopf in agreement with the reversal of the order of the speakers?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I don't have a problem with the reversal of the order. It appears, however, to be advisable to discuss the two distinct issues separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber in its decision thought it would be better to address them separately. So, Mr. Bourgon, let us address them separately. So first let us hear your remarks regarding 89(D), because you were the one who raised the issue. After that, Mr. Dixon will also make his comments, and then the Prosecution will respond and we will have an exchange of opinion. Mr. Bourgon, regarding 89(D), which you have referred to in your documents with respect to a number of the documents, because according to you if those documents are admitted, they would be prejudicial to the accused and it would not be in conformity with Rule 89(D), which I read as follows: "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." And proceeding from this Rule, you listed a number of documents which should be excluded according to you on those grounds. I give you now the floor to elaborate your position.
