I am also going to say that this applies to virtually all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I should like to begin my brief presentation by underlining the fact that indeed almost all the documents proposed by the Prosecution have been X'd by the Defence under the provisions of 89(D), and the Defence has specified that Rule 89(D) was applicable but that the document could be saved through additional evidence, and that is the substance of all our arguments. The arguments of the Defence regarding 89(D) are as follows: As you mentioned, the Chamber should exclude evidence if the probative value of that evidence is significantly outweighed by the needs of a fair trial. In our opinion, this could occur in two instances: First of all, at the moment when the Chamber rules on the admissibility of a document; and secondly, this could occur later, during the assessment by the Chamber of the weight to be attributed to a document which was admitted into evidence within the context of the totality of the evidence. So we would respectfully submit that as far as possible we should exclude documents when they're being tendered, because it is then that the two parties have the chance to convey their respective points of view, which will be entered into the file. The question linked to 89(D) is the following: At what point the probative value of evidence - in this case a document - is largely inferior to the requirements of a fair trial. We certainly cannot enumerate all the situations when such a case may occur, but it is possible, Mr. President, in our view to highlight certain guiding principles which could assist the Chamber in making such a determination. According to the first and simplest scenario, we believe that the accused would be deprived of his right to contradict or cross-examine a document or a witness -- a witness regarding the content of a document. By way of an example, Mr. President: A document is given to the Prosecution by a witness. This witness is called to testify before the Chamber, and during the hearing of that testimony the document is not produced by the Prosecution. As a result, the Defence does not address the matter with the witness, because the Prosecution does not attach any importance to the document. Once the witness goes back home, the Prosecution produces the document, which it had occasion to produce during the testimony of the witness. If the document is accepted by the Chamber, the accused is deprived of his right, which he would have had, to cross-examine the witness who could have had that document admitted. Therefore, according to the weight attached to the document by the Chamber, the burden of proof is reversed and we now have evidence in the file which the accused needs to contradict and explain; whereas, he was deprived of the real opportunity to do that. That is one scenario. And in our opinion, when this occurs, then we could have another witness, but according to this first scenario this document should not be admitted. A second situation - and one that is the most important, in our opinion - is the production of a document which, as it stands, cannot be of assistance to the Chamber. And I shall give you an example: Let us take a document which the Chamber receives. The Chamber, when ruling on its admissibility, has to look at it for relevance, for probative value, but according to our arguments it also should consider the inherent components of these two criteria, and that is reliability. We have already said that reliability is not a separate test nor the first test but reliability still exists and when the Chamber withdraws and looks at the document before it, will the Chamber be able to use that document without asking themselves what that document represents and where it is going according to the Prosecution case? If once they have the document in their possession the Chamber has questions about its reliability, to such an extent that it cannot use that document without engaging in hypothesis about that document, then there is clearly a prejudice to the rights of the accused because the accused did not have occasion to present his arguments on that document, and if the Chamber should be led later on in assessing the documents to giving it weight but the lack of reliability is such that the document does not speak for itself. And we have given several examples of this. When the time comes to assess the ratione temporis of admissibility, we have already heard the arguments of the two parties. I should take advantage of the opportunity to add that contrary to what the Prosecution says I quite agree with my colleague, it is not the date itself that is important; it is the date plus the content. We have to look at the date of the document, the event referred to in the document, and then can one make a determination regarding the relevance of that document. But prima facie a document which falls outside the time frame of the indictment raises the question of whether it should be considered when considering relevance. My learned friend also referred to the matter of the indictment. One should not confuse, Mr. President, the offences alleged in the indictment and the conduct that the two accused are accused of. These are two different things. In the indictment, there are offences which are attributed to certain persons, whether it be Dusina, Miletici, Maljine, or any detention centre. It is alleged that somebody committed an offence there. But what the accused are approached of [as interpreted] are not those offences. We have already said on a number of occasions that the accused are not facing charges of having committed, planned, ordered, aided or abetted in any way the offences alleged in the indictment. What the accused are charged of is their conduct as commanders of not having prevented or punished or taken necessary and reasonable steps to achieve these two objectives; that is, either -- either punishment or prevention. This is quite different from the alleged violations of law. And it is important to underline paragraph 26 of the indictment, which refers to the context within which the Prosecution tends to present its circumstantial case. In paragraph 26, all the municipalities of Central Bosnia are referred to, and this applies to a time frame far before and long after the indictment. But the conduct of which the accused are charged is the conduct of command responsibility between the 31st March, according to the indictment; according to us, it should be the 31st of October, 1993 for General Hadzihasanovic. Therefore, the relevance should be assessed in that way. When we come to reliability, Mr. President, we mentioned yesterday that reliability has several components. In our view, one of the most important components is the authenticity of a document, and authenticity of a document is when the Chamber withdraws to examine a document, will it have the impression that it has before it an authentic document which represents what it says it represents, not whether the content is true but, rather, whether the Chamber will be confident upon reading this document that it will have the necessary information to assess the document. If the Chamber is still questioning it, then this is prejudicial to the accused because he does not have a chance to go back to the document and present his arguments about it. Tomorrow we will have to -- occasion to illustrate what I am saying now because certain documents leave so many questions open to the Chamber regarding the reliability that such a document cannot be admitted without being supported by additional evidence. As my colleague was saying, it's not the end for these documents. They can easily be marked for identification and then during either the Prosecution case or the Defence case or during the proceedings that come after those stages the documents could then be admitted into evidence, and it is only at the end that the Chamber will assess the weight, the probative value to be able to reach a decision in this case. I should like to conclude my presentation, Mr. President, by making two points: First of all, the question of videos. This question is a bit separate from the question of documentary evidence. When a video is produced, one wishes to do two things: To show pictures which correspond to reality; and also a commentary to those pictures, which is a kind of testimony in itself. When we have such a presentation, the reliability of the document is all the more important, since at that point in time we do not have a witness before the Chamber. How can the Chamber attach any probative value to a video, to a picture, if they do not know the source, they do not know the technical characteristics, nor do they know in what way, at what point in time, and for what purpose that video was produced? Earlier on in the course of these proceedings, Mr. President, we had occasion to present arguments about videos. Firstly, we had a video with a scene showing certain men with injuries, and we submitted our arguments at the time to the effect that the scene, which may be in the possession of the Chamber later when they make their determination, should be limited to what was seen during the proceedings and recognised by a witness so as to avoid any prejudice that may be made to the accused when a Chamber would have in their possession a scene that was not part of these adversarial proceedings. That is the first case. The second was with witness Totic. There were arguments by both parties regarding the admissibility of the video. Once the necessary conditions were met, the Defence withdrew its objections to the presentation of a video scene limited in time without any audio commentary, and that video was produced and shown in the courtroom and it is now part of the file. Today we're endeavouring to submit entire videos covering a long period and to have them admitted into evidence en bloc without them having been seen by the Chamber and without the Chamber having any information about this -- these videos. We believe, Mr. President, that this is a real prejudice to the accused unless this prejudice is repaired or annulled with the support of some other evidence, be it testimony, documents, or any other kind of evidence. And the arguments of the Defence focus on the question of the evidence as such, when we're talking about documents, and even more so videos, which are being admitted without any support whatsoever. And I refer to the arguments presented by my colleague, who fully explained the nature of this process. These exhibits were received by the Prosecution, which is one of the three parties to the proceedings. This exhibit, when it was obtained, was not, as is the case in the continental system, already reviewed or analysed before they were admitted into the file by all the parties. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. My last point, Mr. President, has to do with the question addressed by my learned friend from the Prosecution regarding the Kvocka decision. And we are told that evidence can be admitted into evidence and it is up to the Defence to challenge them later on. We are of the opinion that it is quite the opposite and that would absolutely be prejudicial to the accused. If the Chamber is still -- still has questions about a document and its reliability, it cannot admit them under the reservation that the Defence can always challenge that evidence, because in that case there is a reversal of the burden of proof, when it is up to the Defence to challenge evidence; whereas, really it is the Prosecution that needs to produce evidence to support its case, to fulfil its duty of burden of proof beyond any reasonable doubt, and this is up to the Prosecution to do. For those reasons, Mr. President, we request that all the documents for which column 89(D) has been ticked, following the assessment by the Chamber of all the criteria, source, reliability, relevance, probative value, and when all these elements have been -- should be left aside until they are supported with other evidence which would give them an acceptable minimum for the Chamber, and for us the minimum test is whether the Chamber when alone in their chambers assessing a document still have questions about this document, will the document speak for itself to be considered a reliable document or will the Chamber still have questions about it? In that case, this document should not be admitted into evidence. It can be marked for identification, and it can wait for some other occasion when it could be admitted. I'm almost finished, but I forgot to mention something concerning HVO documents. HVO documents, Mr. President, with respect to which the Prosecution has had chance through a witness, witness Totic, to take all the HVO documents it has in its possession and to show them to the witness and to ask him whether this was a document produced by the HVO army: "Do you recognise any signature? Do you recognise any stamp? Do you recognise anything on that document which could assist the Judges to go beyond the threshold of reliability, to answer the minimum questions of the Judges?" But that was not done. And today a whole series of documents is being produced coming from the HVO without a witness, telling the Chamber, "You must understand what the purpose of those documents was, where they come from, and everything else." My last point has to do with the external character of documents. The external character of documents, Mr. President, is that the further removed a document is from the accused, the more -- the higher the standard of reliability should be. The closer the document is to the accused, then the question of reliability is less for the Chamber. Before using a document produced by another army in another headquarters which had the ambitions of being the enemy of the accused, then that document must have a minimum reliability. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now summarise what you have just said, and then Mr. Withopf may take the floor to respond to your case. If necessary, you can also respond to the Prosecution, and then Mr. Dixon can comment on Rule 89(D). Your presentation was very detailed. I'll just go through the main points. Naturally the Prosecution will have to inform us of its position. You addressed a key issue and you stated that the Trial Chamber must rule when documents are being admitted into evidence. This is the position that you expressed when documents are being admitted, and the Trial Chamber has to assess and deliberate, according to the Rules, it's when a document is being tendered that you believe that the Trial Chamber should assess the probative value of the document and also the need to ensure a fair trial. At that point in time, if the Trial Chamber deems that the probative value is outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial, the document should be excluded. Your position is quite clear. You then addressed a second issue, which is also of crucial importance. You stated that there are certain guidelines that have to be followed in order to ensure a fair trial. Everyone is familiar with them. And this concerns the right that the accused has to cross-examine a witness. And on that basis, you asked yourself a question: When witnesses appear, the Prosecution can tender documents. If they had done so at that moment, you would have cross-examined the witness about the document in question. This was not done. To tender a document into evidence after a witness has been heard is prejudicial to the accused, given that you were not in a position to cross-examine the witness with regard to the document, and thus the accused's rights are not respected. That was the second important problem that you mentioned. There was a third point that you dealt with, and that concerned the Trial Chamber's role with regard to the examination of documents and with regard to document reliability. You said that when the Trial Chamber deliberates, the Trial Chamber may find that it has certain questions about documents that concern the reliability of the documents, and if the Defence was not able to provide the Chamber with certain clarifications, in such a case this might be prejudicial to the accused. That was the third topic that you addressed, the prejudice that might be caused to the accused when the Chamber examines documents that are not reliable, documents which have been admitted. You then addressed the issue of ratione temporis, and you stated that a document consists of a date and its contents. It's not just the contents or the date that constitutes the document. You should assess the document by taking into account both the contents and the date of the document. That was another issue that you dealt with. You then mentioned a more legal issue, which is the criminal responsibility of the accused. You pointed out that if there are certain allegations in the indictment concerning offences in municipalities - you mentioned Dusina, et cetera - but you said that the offences, the crimes in these municipalities weren't crimes committed by the accused. What the accused are charged with is not having prevented or punished these crimes. That's the meaning of Article 7(3). That's what they are charged with, the fact of not having prevented the crime or punished the crime. These are the crimes covered by Article 7(3) of the Statute. And you wanted to remind us of this legal issue. You then addressed, again, the issue of reliability, and you asked how the Trial Chamber could assess the authenticity of a document if certain elements regarding its authenticity were missing. You stated that if the Trial Chamber ruled and mentioned the question of an authentic document without the Prosecution having been able to provide the Trial Chamber with sufficient information, in such a case this could be prejudicial to the accused. You said that it was your intention to refer to certain documents tomorrow that deal with this issue. You then dealt with certain other important issues. You mentioned the problem of videos. You mentioned two videos that have been admitted, the Totic video and the video concerning wounded witnesses, and in your opinion the videos should be shown to the Trial Chamber in order to enable the Defence to express its position and to ensure a fair trial for the accused. To admit videos without showing them would be a grave violation of the accused's rights. You said that a video consists of images and a commentary, and naturally it is necessary for the Defence to be able to express its position with regard to the video. You again addressed the issue of the Kvocka decision, and you stated that the implementation of this decision would be a matter of reversing the burden of proof. The Defence would have to be contesting certain evidence, whereas it is for the Prosecution to prove its case. Applying this decision by saying that one will admit this and then by saying that the Defence has to contest what will is being admitted, in your opinion doing this amounts to reversing the burden of proof. You then dealt with the issue of HVO documents. You expressed surprise because when General Totic was present the Prosecution didn't consider it necessary to show him the so-called HVO documents, because this high-ranking member of the military could have identified the documents at that point in time, yet this was not done. Finally, you redefined - this is something you said yesterday, but you repeated it today - you addressed the issue of the external examination of documents. You claimed that the further removed a document was from the accused, the greater the guarantees should be concerning the reliability of the document. On the other hand, if the document was issued by the accused or closer to the accused, in such a case the guarantees of reliability need not be so great. So all these comments are very interesting, and it is necessary for the Prosecution to respond so that the Trial Chamber can be aware of the situation before deliberating. I will now give Mr. Dixon the floor and we will continue. It's better to follow such a procedure. It will be clearer for everyone, rather than mixing up the arguments of both parties. So I will give the floor to Mr. Withopf now. Could you comment on all the issues addressed by Mr. Bourgon. I summarise that in order to cover all the issues raised. But, Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I'm in agreement with my learned friend from the Kubura Defence that it may be appropriate, with the Chamber's permission, that the Kubura Defence comments on the two issues in question and then the Prosecution can respond just once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you would prefer Mr. Dixon to take the floor now. If he's going to say the same things, that might be useful; but if he has other elements to add, that might cause certain confusion for the public and also for the Trial Chamber. Mr. Dixon, would you be repeating what Mr. Bourgon said? What would you like to do? Would you like to comment now, or would you rather have the Prosecution respond to Mr. Bourgon at this point in time and then respond to what you have to say? It seems that the Prosecution thinks that you should take the floor now and then the Prosecution could respond. But perhaps they're interpreting your position. What would you -- how would you like to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further to add to Mr. Bourgon's very thorough submission on Rule 89(D), so on that topic we have nothing further to add. I do have some brief submissions on the question of witness requirements, but I'm not sure if that's going to be dealt with separately after 89(D). If it is, then I will wait until after Mr. Withopf has responded on 89(D) and then make further submissions on witness requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So now we are dealing with 89(D). The question that concerns witness requirements is the last issue to be dealt with, and it's an essential question because we have to know which documents can only be tendered through witnesses. I think that that is what you wanted to comment on. So the best way to proceed, as the Trial Chamber has said, is for Mr. Withopf to respond to Mr. Bourgon's submissions, given that Mr. Kubura's Defence has adopted more or less the same position as the Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's the understanding of the Prosecution that our learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence actually addressed both issues, Rule 89(D) and the issue of the necessary to have witnesses. That's at least our interpretation of what has been discussed. If I may, please, first address Rule 89(D). This is a very distinct issue, and we have done research on the ICTY's jurisprudence on this issue. The research has revealed the following: This Rule has not -- has not occasioned extensive jurisprudence. What, however, transpired is the following, and this is summarising the jurisprudence of the ICTY. The probative value of evidence is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial in cases in which the Defence did not have sufficient time to properly prepare the defence or, if the materials the Prosecution wishes to be tendered into evidence, were obtained contrary to internationally protected human rights. As it is quite obvious, this jurisprudence touches on the issues which are relied -- related to the irregularity of the proceedings, which is quite different from the Defence submissions on this issue. The ICTY's jurisprudence in addition covers two other scenarios. Number one would be documents that are of cumulative nature only; and number two, the evidence would be hearsay evidence only. That means none -- none of the criteria, or none of these four or five criteria apply to the documents Defence wishes to have excluded from admission into evidence for the reasons they explained today. In this context, I wish to emphasise that this trial is conducted before professional Judges, who are certainly in a position to judge on the issues related to Rule 89(D). If I may briefly address the issue of the videos. The videos in many instances -- and the Prosecution invites the Trial Chamber to actually view the videos, and they can be made available. The videos in many instances are quite self-explanatory. They are quite self-explanatory by the fact what can be seen on the video and what is written on the footage, which is sometimes quite interesting to know. That means the concern that a witness is necessarily needed to assess the probative value of a video is not -- at least not in all instances, shared by the Prosecution. My learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence has also addressed the issue why the Prosecution hasn't shown Brigadier Totic all documents that stem from the HVO. Brigadier Totic at the time in 1993 was a brigade commander. He would not have been in a position to comment on any HVO documents that fall outside the scope of his responsibilities at the time. Therefore, it wouldn't have made sense to introduce all HVO documents via this particular witness. As I said, the Prosecution understands, at least from what my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence submitted today, that he also addressed the issue whether witnesses are necessary to admit documents into evidence, and therefore with the permission of the Trial Chamber I would like to continue with this issue. The issue has been addressed on a number of occasions before this Trial Chamber. Having had a close look at the written submissions of the Defence, it appears that the Defence wishes to have for the vast majority of the materials, if not for all of them, a witness being questioned in respect to them. To summarise the Prosecution's position, it has been accepted in the past by at least two Trial Chambers - the Galic and the Simic Trial Chamber - that documents can be tendered from the bar table not using a witness. This is in full compliance with the procedures and practices applied in civil-law jurisdictions. The only issue, Mr. President, Your Honours, the only issue which in the submission of the Prosecution can be discussed is the issue of the probative value of documents which are tendered without a witness for the reasons that documents not having been discussed with a witness did not receive the scrutiny involved in the cross-examination of a witness. In this context, Mr. President, Your Honours, reference is made to the Celebici Trial Chamber decision of 19th of January, 1998, and in particular to its paragraph 22, where it says: "It is clear from the relevant provisions of the Rules that there's no blanket prohibition on the admission of documents simply on the ground that their purported author had not been called to testify in the proceedings." And they continue to say: "It is a different matter that the probative value of such evidence by necessary will be affected by the fact that it has not received the scrutiny involved in the cross-examination of a witness." This is an important factor to which the Trial Chamber will give due consideration at the stage of assessing the weight to be attached to exhibits of this nature. Again, this is paragraph 22 of the Celebici Trial Chamber decision of 19th of January, 1998, which to its full extent summarises the Prosecution's view on this issue. And this is exactly the reason, Mr. President, Your Honours, why the Prosecution certainly will continue to discuss certain documents with witnesses in order to ensure that such documents and the contents of such documents and that the probative value of the contents of such documents is at the disposal and is known to the Trial Chamber to the extent possible. The situation expressed in the Celebici Trial Chamber decision of 19th January 1998 obviously covers two distinct situations; namely, a witness is not called, or a witness has been withdrawn, as it happened in respect to the one witness whose name was redacted from the transcript earlier on today; and the second situation, a witness was called but has not for whatever reason been questioned about a document this witness may have been provided. These are the submissions, Mr. President, Your Honours, in respect to the two issues, Rule 89(D) and the issue as to whether witnesses have to be questioned in respect to all documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we have our necessary break, I'll summarise what you have just said, and then the Defence can take the floor after the break. You said that in view of the issues raised by the Defence you studied the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, and if I have understood you correctly, the jurisprudence doesn't -- is not very extensive and doesn't enlighten us greatly, but you can distinguish two types of jurisprudence. There's the question of cumulative evidence, and there's the question of hearsay evidence. But in spite of this, you said that the difficulties we may encounter could be dealt with given that we have professional Judges here, who are in a position to assess the relevance, the probative value, the reliability of documents, et cetera, et cetera. You also pointed out that there were three decisions - the Galic and Simic decision - in these two decisions, it is said that it is possible to tender documents into evidence without having recourse to a witness, so there is no need for the Defence's arguments; they have no ground. This has already been ruled on. You also mentioned the Celebici decision dated the 19th of January, 1998, and you referred to paragraph 22 of that decision. This paragraph states that if a document was not one with regard to which a witness could be cross-examined by the Defence, the Trial Chamber in such a case draws the conclusion that the probative value of the document in question is not as great; it is diminished. On the basis of this Celebici decision, you said that the Prosecution will be introducing documents through witnesses in the future, in the weeks to come. So there was a question that I was asking myself: Should what you said be interpreted to mean that some of the documents on the list, some of the documents that have been contested, are going to be tendered into evidence through witnesses? If that is the case, it would be very useful for us to know about this as soon as possible. And this would enable us to avoid unnecessary debate. Unless we're dealing with witnesses who will be appearing with documents that are not on the list, but this is not something that I could even imagine. So, Mr. Withopf, could you be more precise about what you meant. As far as I'm concerned - but I think this is what the other Judges understood too - you said that in future witnesses will be appearing and you will be tendering documents into evidence through these witnesses, bearing in mind the Celebici decision, naturally. But these documents are already on the list. Is that correct? What can you tell us about this? And we will then adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, to be very clear in that respect, the Prosecution wishes to have tendered all documents on its current list into evidence based on the discussions -- on the ongoing discussions. In order and in respect to the probative value, however, the Prosecution intends to discuss a certain number of documents which the Prosecution wishes to have been tendered into evidence by a future decision of the Trial Chamber, based on the yesterday's, today's, and tomorrow's discussion, will discuss such documents with witnesses as has been done in the past with respect to a number of documents which were not contested by the Defence and went into evidence based on a Trial Chamber's decision. So the Prosecution wishes to have all documents, as suggested, to be admitted into evidence. However, the Prosecution in the future will discuss a certain number of such documents in addition with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I'll summarise what you said. You said that you're requesting that all the documents be admitted into evidence, and you said that some of these documents - we don't know which ones at this point of time - some of these documents could be the subject of debate with witnesses. That is how we have understood you. We will now adjourn. It is 12.32. We will resume at 1.00 and we will then conclude the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following what we have been told by Mr. Withopf, does Mr. Bourgon have any remarks to make in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My comments would be divided into two parts, Mr. President. First of all, I should like to respond to the arguments offered by the Prosecution regarding the question of 89(D) of the Rules; and secondly, I will address the second point, that is, the question of the necessity of calling a witness. Regarding the point made by the Prosecution connected to 89(D) concerning video evidence, and the Prosecution tells us that they are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. self-explanatory, and it is interesting also to see the footage that may be included on the video. My friend himself underlined the danger of seeing this video. Who is telling us that that video is the truth? Who tells us when it was taken? Who tells us that it is not a fabrication? Without having technical knowledge, we all know how easily montages can be made and the clippings combined from different periods, different dates, and different places. Regarding the footage at the bottom of the screen, who wrote those comments? Are they truthful? For what purpose were they included in the video? All these points speak in favour of having a video being introduced through a witness and not simply given in the course of these proceedings. The second point, Mr. President, has to do with witness Totic. My learned friend did not appear to understand the point I made concerning the documents through this witness. Of course, Mr. President, it would not have been possible for witness Totic to speak of the contents of those documents, unless he himself was implicated, and surely the Prosecution in that case would have used those documents. But that was not the point made by the Defence. Our question had to do with reliability. We believe, as we are going to show tomorrow, that these HVO documents are so little reliable in themselves that they cannot be admitted into evidence as such. Witness Totic could have identified how the documents were drafted, how they were sent, how they were received, the numbering applied, who can or cannot sign such documents, so he could have provided a great deal of information to the Chamber and thereby increased the reliability of all HVO documents, perhaps even beyond the threshold which we respectfully ask the Chamber to respect. So that was the purpose of my comments regarding witness Totic. Finally, the last point, Mr. President, made by my learned friend, and he said that if a document is introduced into evidence and -- sorry, I'll start again. The document is in the file. A witness appears, and the Defence does not address that document with the witness. It would appear, according to my learned friend, that the presumption would be that the document has no interest for the Defence and that the Defence does not object regarding the reliability and relevance of that document. It would appear that it is up to the Defence to raise the question of a document with a witness. Mr. President, the procedure in this Tribunal is clear; the burden of proof is with the Prosecution and not the Defence. The argument of the Defence is quite the opposite. The Prosecution received a document from a witness, and when that witness appears before the Chamber, they don't use that document. So in that case, we believe that the presumption must be that the document has no probative value, otherwise it would have been used. It is their purpose, their aim, their burden of proof to say that the document could be admitted later and if the Defence didn't address the document with the witness, that is again a reversal of the burden of proof and that is prejudicial to the accused. Those are my comments regarding the first part of the presentation regarding 89(D). I now come to the second part of my comments, that is, the need to have a witness present to be able to introduce a document. The first comment is something that we have said repeatedly. We do not believe that there is any rule which says that the document cannot be produced in itself. This exists in all jurisdictions, common law and civil law. There are conditions when a document may be admitted. That is not the argument of the Defence. The argument of the Defence is that if there is a problem with a document, in that case the document can only -- cannot be produced in itself and by itself. My learned friend refers to a decision in Celebici, where it said, I think, that that were no blanket prohibition. I think this is the term he used. I don't have the whole paragraph, but if my understanding is correct, the question had to do with the author of the document and we quite agree with that decision. One doesn't always need to have the author of the document, but one may need some other witness to give sufficient probative value to a document so that it exceeds the necessary threshold. We agree that the author of a document doesn't have to testify on each and every occasion. When determining whether a witness is necessary or not, there are two cases: The case of admissibility and the case of substance. When we are talking about admissibility, that is, when we have to see whether a document is admissible, the argument of the Defence is, as we already said, that some documents necessitate something in addition, something additional, and that something, Mr. President, could be, by way of example, another document, perhaps a witness, a witness who is not the author, a witness who could throw -- shed some light on that document. But there are also other possibilities and that would add sufficiently to reliability to make the document admissible. When the Chamber sees the examples we will discuss tomorrow, you will be able to see that for many documents when marked by an "X" for a witness, they could also be supported by other evidence, because this was a question of admissibility and all we wanted to make sure was that the document was reliable. Also, there are certain documents which require more than that, which obligatorily require a witness, in our view. And we refer to Article -- to Rule 92 bis of the Rules. 92 bis was designed to allow written statements to be admitted instead of testimony without having had the witness to come, to stand in for oral testimony. But this is done under certain circumstances. And we are told in Rule 92 bis, among other things, that Rule 92 bis -- or 92 bis testimony in writing would be encouraged in the following circumstances, and we are told: "The factors in favour of admitting evidence in the form of a written statement include cumulative nature, historical, political, or military background; containing statistical analysis of the ethnic composition; concerning the impact of crimes upon victims; relating to issues of the character of the accused; or relating to factors to be taken into account in determining sentence." However, we are told that there are factors against admitting evidence in written form. And in -- paragraph A it says: "There is an overriding public interest in the evidence in question being presented orally." And B: "When a party objecting can demonstrate that its nature and source renders it unreliable or that its prejudicial effect outweighs its probative value." And finally: "There are any other factors which make it appropriate for the witness to appear." There are factors that are in favour and factors that are against, but there is one determining factor; that is, those that refer to the accused. It has to be proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment. Therefore, we are talking about testimony here in 92 bis, but we must look at the spirit of this Rule. A written statement is not replacing oral evidence when it relates to acts and conduct of the accused. Also, a document cannot be tendered without a witness if it relates to the acts and conduct of the accused, because that would be contrary with the letter and spirit of 92 bis. Therefore, our argument regarding documents that absolutely require a witness are the documents which relate to the acts and conduct of the accused. Among those documents, Mr. President, there are documents bearing the signature of the accused that were drafted by the accused, ordered by the accused, or that directly relate to the acts and conduct of the accused. In spite of that, Mr. President, as we noted yesterday, we have withdrawn all challenge to a number of documents that were signed by the accused, clearly to allow the effective progress of the proceedings. However, when we come to admissibility and we ticked the box "witness", that means the document may be supported with a witness or other documents, but when they relate to the acts and conduct of the accused, there must be a witness. Then there's another point: When my learned friend spoke about the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. And as we do not fit into that jurisprudence, therefore we should be rejected. If he found jurisprudence which rejected the arguments of the Defence, then that would be applicable, but the way they put it, I think it is turning upside down the use of jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On the question of the requirements for witnesses, there are two general points which I want to make before going into some specific categories that we have identified for where witnesses, in our submission, are required. The first general point is that yes, Your Honours have noted that all of the witnesses where there is a document have been crossed in order to indicate that all documents essentially require a witness. There's an important clarification here, the first being that as was indicated yesterday, we do require - and the Prosecution has conceded to this - a witness from the various archives to explain how the documents arrived in the archives, as Your Honour pointed out, what happened between 1993 and 2000, when the archives were searched by the Prosecution. As I outlined yesterday in relation to the archive for the 7th Brigade, there are some questions that we have about when in fact that archive existed and how the documents came to be located in that archive. And that's one of the reasons why all the witnesses have been crossed, because most of the documents relate to one or other of those archives. But it doesn't mean that we would have to have 600 witnesses. It might mean a single witness for an archive which would cross out a number of documents, possibly two, 300 of those documents. Secondly, Your Honours, it may well be that even though a number of documents have been crossed for a witness, when they are looked at in categories - and I'm going to come on to these categories now - it will not be necessary to have a witness for each and every document but one witness could deal with a number of documents in a category. We are committed to seeking to only require the minimum amount of witnesses to come in order that the documents can be fully assessed with those witnesses. It will not be necessary to conceive of this as a process that is going to substantially lengthen the Prosecution case. Indeed, we -- we have just over a month and a half still of court time, given the Prosecution's estimation, within which some additional witnesses could be called to address these documents. We have identified, Your Honours, seven categories where we would require a witness, and it might well be that there are only a handful of witnesses in each category, possibly even a single witness, to cover the documents concerned. But much will depend on the documents and the kinds of witnesses that the Prosecution may seek to call, and that is of course a matter for them in presenting their case. The first category is headed "The signature of Mr. Kubura." There are a handful of documents, about eight or nine documents, which we say although Mr. Kubura's name appears on the bottom of the document, the signature above it is not his. And this can easily be ascertained by comparing those signatures with his signature on a number of other documents which the Prosecution has not -- sorry, which the Defence has not placed in dispute. Some of those documents where we say the signature is wrong, it's not his signature, are signed by other persons, some of which may be identifiable but others not. And in respect of those orders, we insist on a witness being called to explain who signed those orders, it being paramount that they are not associated with Mr. Kubura, as he was not the person who issued those orders. If a witness cannot be provided, then in our submission it would be highly prejudicial to accept the document into evidence when it is plain on its face that it is not his signature, in comparison to the signatures on other documents. The second category is headed "Signatures of others, or third parties." These are documents signed not by Mr. Kubura or somebody purportedly signing for him but other members of the 7th Brigade, or the 3rd Corps, or persons outside of the 3rd Corps where we have no knowledge of whether the signature on the document is indeed the signature of the person concerned and no knowledge of the document itself. Here we also insist that a witness or group of witnesses should be called, especially given that the authors of these documents were serving members of either the HVO or the Bosnian army at the time. They are readily available in Bosnia and could be called to verify, or not, the document concerned. It would not be a question of days and days of testimony. It might even simply be taking a statement from them, where they identify the document, and there may be no further challenge from the Defence thereafter, depending on the contents of that statement. These are all procedures that would have been undertaken, to revert to my previous point, either by an investigating judge in a civil-law system, or by the police or prosecutor's office in a common-law system, to verify that these are authentic documents and to confirm the signature on them, especially when they are not the signatures of the accused persons. The third category is headed "Handwritten documents." And there are about a dozen of these, which are documents that are not official, no stamps appear on them, handwritten in -- in handwritings that are not clear to the Defence who they belong to, and where the author of the document in some cases is not known. The same considerations that apply to the previous category would apply to this; that those documents should be excluded unless they can be verified by the author or by somebody within the armed forces who can confirm the existence of these documents. The fourth category are, "Witnesses who are still to come," a matter which Your Honours have raised. The very first document on the Prosecution list is a document that is a transcript about a conversation between Mr. Hogg and a certain Mr. Aziz. Mr. Hogg is on the Prosecution list of witnesses still to be called, and in our view documents like this should not be introduced into evidence until the witness is called, and when the witness is called the document can be sought to be introduced through that witness. There are a number of these documents, documents where witnesses are still to attend, and we are at a loss as to why the Prosecution does simply not wait for those witnesses to come and introduce them in the normal manner. The next category is one headed "El-Liva magazine," which is allegedly the mouthpiece of the 7th Brigade, a fact which is disputed by the Defence. Many of these magazine entries or journal entries come from a period very late in the day after the indictment in 1994/1995, and Your Honours know what our objection is in respect of such documents. But in addition to that, we would require a witness - and it might only be a single witness - to testify about the nature of this magazine. Where did they get their information from, how did it come to end up in the magazine, and what was the status of this magazine, whether it was indeed one that had anything to do with the 7th Brigade. The next category which has been mentioned on a number of occasions is headed "Videos." Your Honours know what our objections are in respect of the videos. To give just but one additional example, contested exhibit number 409 is a video where the source is unknown, and the Prosecution has also indicated "sensitive source." The date of the video is 21 August 1992, and the document description is: "A videotape of the formation of the ABiH 3rd Corps, 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in 1992 in Travnik municipality." The Prosecution has indicated today, and indeed in paragraph 19 of the indictment, the allegation is that the 7th Brigade formed on 19 November 1992, and yet here we have a video which was supposedly taken in August 1992 regarding the formation of the 7th Brigade. Your Honours will appreciate why we are contesting the reliability of such a videotape and why we require a witness to explain how they were videoing this formation when in fact the Prosecution's own case is that the 7th Brigade was formed some two to three months later. And then the final category are documents where there's no signature on the document whatsoever. The Prosecution gave some explanation yesterday why that might be the case. But as we indicated yesterday, it's not for the Prosecution to give that evidence. We need a witness to explain why they are documents that are unsigned so that Your Honours can assess whether any value can be attached to such documents. Your Honour, those are the seven categories where we indicate that witnesses are required. We will tomorrow present examples from those seven categories in order to attempt to illustrate to Your Honours what kinds of documents we are talking about and why we require a witness for them. In addition, if Your Honours so request, we can provide a breakdown of which documents fit into which category so that it's absolutely clear which are the documents that are contested under these different headings and that it will not be necessary, then, to go back to the whole long consolidated list and try and make out what the objections are. It might be more convenient to have the documents listed under these different headings with some examples given for Your Honours in order that a decision can be made about whether witnesses should be called for them or whether indeed they should be excluded, if no witness is available or even if a witness comes, the document is irrelevant in any event. Your Honour, there's one final category. It's a general one. There are just two documents for completeness which I wish to -- to mention. And that is the prior testimony of Colonel Stewart, number 57 on the consolidated exhibit list. I understand that that is still sought to be relied upon by the Prosecution, even though they've withdrawn the prior testimonies of a number of other witnesses. In our submission, that document -- or that testimony cannot be admitted without Colonel Stewart being made available because it is testimony that goes to the acts and conduct of the accused, and accordingly 92 bis would require him to. And then there's one other document which Your Honours will be familiar with, document number 58, which is the so-called "Instructions to Muslim fighters." This document is marked for identification already. The Prosecution sought to introduce it through a member of the 7th Brigade but was unable to do so, and in our view that document should not be admitted unless a witness can identify the document and give it its necessary reliability, if that indeed exists. This is an important document because the Prosecution has alleged that it was used widely throughout the 7th Brigade and 3rd Corps, but at the moment it's not a document in evidence, and that is one where we would certainly require a witness to attend. Your Honour, I hope that has been of some assistance. We will provide examples tomorrow and can provide the document numbers under those headings in order to assist Your Honours in deciding these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf may take the floor now. I will summarise what you said. First I will provide you with a summary of what Defence counsel said, what Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Dixon said. Mr. Bourgon went back to a certain number of problems concerning Rule 89(D) and he mentioned Rule 92 bis. He argued that the spirit of Rule 92 bis, in the case of statements, but this could also be applied to documents, when we're dealing with the dates and the conduct of the accused, in such cases we need a witness according to the spirit of the Rule. Mr. Bourgon made a comparison with questions that had to do with reliability. Mr. Dixon then expressed his position. He mentioned seven categories of documents, and he provided us with a number of examples, which I won't go through, as everyone was following what was said. By way of example, I'll mention category 2, which concerns documents that were signed by third parties and not by the person who was supposed to sign the document. And the Defence believes that we require to have as a witness the person who actually signed the document. Mr. Dixon also stated that witnesses will be appearing and that when they do so, documents could be tendered into evidence. He mentioned the journalist Hogg within the framework of the conversation -- the interview he had with Mr. Aziz. Another category, another example given concerned the 7th Brigade magazine. I have it before me. It has a stamp with a coat of arms of the BH Republic, but it's the 1st of March, 1994. That's the date. Perhaps there are other magazines, but the Defence told us that it would be good to have a witness who could authenticate such documents. And Mr. Dixon mentioned something that was also mentioned yesterday. He said that it was necessary to call archivists to testify before the Tribunal. The Trial Chamber noted that the Defence suggests to -- suggest that they make a document which would divide the documents into these seven categories. Naturally, anything that might help clarify matters and anything that might assist us is very welcome. It's not necessary to render a decision to that effect. This is something that the parties can do spontaneously, given that this could assist the Chamber and the other party. Generally speaking, such were the positions expressed by the Defence. As the burden of proof is placed on the Prosecution, I will for one last time let them take the floor again. We will then adjourn. The hearing will resume tomorrow, and we will examine the 50 documents that were mentioned. Mr. Withopf, you may take floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Taking into account the time that has passed by, I will keep my observations very short. I first address Rule 92 bis. Rule 92 bis is obviously made in respect to written witness statements. There's a difference obviously between written witness statements and documents and the fact that documents are not -- are deliberately not included within the scope of Rule 92 bis makes it pretty obvious that documents do not have to match the criteria under Rule 92 bis, even in the event in which the contents of the documents go to the acts and the conduct of the accused. It's the submission of the Prosecution that the gist of Rule 92 bis cannot be used in respect to documents because documents are a completely different category of evidence, as in comparison to witness statements, written witness statements. As mentioned earlier on, the Prosecution does agree and will take efforts to either call the archivists of the archives as witnesses or to take Rule 92 bis statements. My learned friend from the Kubura Defence mentioned a number of categories which they think the documents should be dealt with. Again, this issue touches on the basic issue whether it's a question of admissibility or a question of probative value. If there is no signature, the Prosecution would tend to agree that the probative value is less in comparison to a document on which is a signature. In respect to the very particular example which has been given by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence, the fact that a military order which has the name at the very bottom, the name of the accused Kubura at the very bottom, however it's signed by somebody else, does not exclude by any means that the accused Kubura issued the order and somebody else signed at his behalf. Again, the Prosecution considers this category, as all other categories, being an issue of probative value, not an issue of admissibility of documents. The "El-Liva" magazine has already been addressed by Your Honour, the Presiding Judge. The "El-Liva" magazine - and I have a copy in front of me - prima facie it's obviously an official magazine by the 7th Muslim Brigade. It has the stamps and all the essentials of the Armija Republic of BiH on it, and on its face it is obviously an official document. In respect to the video which the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber about, that there is a sensitive source, if the Trial Chamber requests, particularly requests to reveal the name of the sensitive source, the Prosecution is prepared to reveal the name in closed session. To summarise the Prosecution's submission, many of the issues addressed do not have to do with the issue of admissibility of documents but with the issue of probative value. The documents have to be seen in their totality because in some areas this case is a case of circumstantial evidence, and the Prosecution again wishes to emphasise that it suggests that the Trial Chamber applies the procedure as it has been applied for good reasons by the Kvocka Trial Chamber. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will now adjourn, since all the items on the agenda have been covered, with the exception of the 50 documents, which accounts for 10 per cent of the totality of documents, roughly speaking. These documents will be examined tomorrow. We will examine them one by one, and this will enable us to progress and have an overall view of the situation. Before we adjourn, I would nevertheless like to remind both parties, and in particular the Defence, that the need for a fair trial means that the accused naturally must be represented by Defence counsel and must also be in a position to contest the evidence presented by the Prosecution. This should take place within the framework of adversarial proceedings. This is what it means to have a fair trial. The Defence and the accused must be in a position to express their position and have a view of the evidence used against the accused. So this is a general principle which must always be present in the minds of both parties. Having said that, on that basis, something that everyone should remember is that it is necessary to know whether the accused had time to examine the documents and to express their opinion of the documents. As you are well aware, this case didn't start a few months ago but a few years ago, because the indictment was issued some time ago. Since the indictment was issued, the Prosecution has disclosed to the Defence most of the documents. The Defence has been able to assess the documents together with the accused. When the Trial Chamber asked the Defence to present their arguments, the Defence was in a position to inform us about issues that had to do with authenticity, relevance, reliability, unknown sources, et cetera, and they could do this for each single document, which means that adversarial -- an adversarial debate had already been engaged. This debate will continue tomorrow. We will be dealing with the 50 documents mentioned. I wanted to remind you of this, bearing in mind what has been said today. We will now adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00. We will adjourn tomorrow around 1.45, and the Judges will then have to render a decision with regard to the oral and written request presented by the Prosecution, the request that concerns tendering these documents into evidence. Thank you, and I will see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
